proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 7 waives consequential damages but sets no cap, so both parties' direct liability is unlimited; we add our standard mutual cap at the greater of 12 months' amounts under the Agreement and USD 1,000,000. ops.text: (b) Except with respect to Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of (i) the amounts paid or payable between the Parties under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim and (ii) USD 1,000,000. "Excluded Claims" means a Party's breach of its confidentiality, data protection or security obligations, its indemnification obligations, its gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, and its infringement of the other Party's intellectual property rights. Amounts owed by a Party under Section 5 (Fees and Payment) shall not be treated as damages subject to this limitation.

proposal.summary: Add a mutual liability cap with standard uncapped carve-outs to Section 7

rationale: Section 7 contains only a mutual waiver of consequential/indirect damages (carved out for indemnification and breach of confidentiality); no monetary cap on liability appears in Section 7 or anywhere else in the document (searches for "aggregate", "exceed" and "Fees" return no cap language). The fallback requires a mutual cap of 12 months' fees with carve-outs, so the absence of any cap fails the fallback on a material term and leaves our own direct liability unlimited. Because this is a revenue-share arrangement in which Customer pays no fees to Kubient (Section 5: payment flows from Kubient to Customer), a pure "fees paid by Customer" basis would be illusory; the redline therefore adopts the preferred greater-of formulation using amounts paid or payable between the Parties and a USD 1,000,000 floor, adds the standard uncapped carve-outs, and confirms revenue-share amounts owed are not "damages" for cap purposes. The existing consequential-damages waiver is mutual and acceptable and is left intact.

quote: Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party. Except for termination for material breach as detailed in paragraph 4(b), Kubient shall be entitled to all fees generated during the termination period regardless of which Party terminates the Agreement
rationale: Compliant at the fallback; no redline and no counterparty comment proposed. A Customer convenience right is present and enforceable by us. The preamble (p0000) defines The Associated Press as the "Customer" and provides that "Each of Customer and Kubient may be referred to herein individually as a 'Party'", so the Section 4(a) grant that "Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other Party" expressly confers a for-any-reason (convenience) exit on AP. The deterministic "Customer convenience termination present" check fails only because the sentence uses the defined term "Party" instead of naming the Customer; that is a drafting-phrasing artifact and does not affect the substance. Notice period: 90 days, squarely inside the fallback's 60-90 day window. Term: a one (1) year Initial Term auto-renewing in 1-year increments, so the trigger for "absence of any Customer convenience right in a term longer than 12 months" is not met and there is no multi-year lock-in. Vendor side: Kubient's convenience right requires the same 90 days' notice - not "fewer than 90 days" - so the walk-away threshold is not reached, the right is symmetric rather than one-sided against us, and the Initial Term bar prevents Kubient exiting mid-term. Economics: Kubient's entitlement to fees "generated during the termination period" is bounded by the ~3-month notice period rather than being an uncapped early-termination penalty, consistent with the fallback cap of no more than 3 months' fees, and it applies whichever party terminates. Noted per the minor sub-element rule, not flagged: 90 days rather than the preferred 30; Kubient's right not confined to term-end; and no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund, which is inapplicable because Section 5 is a revenue-share under which Kubient remits to AP rather than AP prepaying fees.

Evidence of absence: the document is a single flat section, so there is no separate restrictive-covenants or general-provisions section in which a covenant could sit. The independent contractor clause (p0066) disclaims an employment relationship but imposes no hiring or solicitation restriction, so it creates no implied covenant. The quoted survival list at p0070 enumerates confidentiality, proprietary rights, indemnification, limitations of liability, effects of termination and governing law, and omits any non-solicit, confirming none exists to survive.

The deterministic checks for duration (12 months or less) and for a general-solicitation carve-out are inapplicable, and their failure is not evidence of an error: both measure the wording of an existing non-solicit, and there is none in this Agreement to measure. Neither Party may terminate this Agreement during the Initial Term except as set forth in paragraph 4(b) or any Exhibit. Pricing is a revenue share set in the Exhibits with no unilateral uplift mechanic, so the CPI/3% cap is not engaged; the absence of a vendor renewal reminder is a minor sub-element only and is not separately flagged.

As drafted, Section 4(c)(iv) lets Kubient simply destroy our information, which leaves us unable to migrate; we can accept a 90-day assistance period if six months is difficult.

proposal.summary: Insert post-termination transition assistance and data-return obligation in Section 4(c)

quote: (iv) and each Party will return or destroy any of the other Party's Confidential Information then in its possession.
rationale: Section 4(c) is the only effect-of-termination provision: Kubient ceases the Services, the licence is revoked, Customer stops using the Auction Platform, and each Party may "return or destroy" the other's Confidential Information at its own election. There is no transition-assistance obligation and no right for AP to receive its Content, Requests or other data back in a usable format, and no deletion certification; searches for transition/migration/export/data-return language return nothing elsewhere in the Agreement. Because Kubient could elect destruction, this sits at or near the walk-away position (no data return / immediate deletion), failing even the fallback (90 days' assistance plus export within 30 days). We therefore insert a new paragraph 4(c)(v) reflecting the preferred position — up to six months' assistance at then-current rates, machine-readable return within 30 days, then deletion with written certification — expressly overriding the destroy option for Customer Data, and flag the 90-day fallback in the comment.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return

verification.notes: The rule expects a transition-assistance and data-return clause; the only effect-of-termination provision (4(c)(i)-(iv)) covers cessation of services, licence revocation and a mutual 'return or destroy' election for Confidential Information, with no transition assistance, no data export in a usable format and no deletion certification — 'missing' is the correct classification and not double-flagged elsewhere. The inserted 4(c)(v) tracks the playbook model language closely (six months' assistance at then-current rates, machine-readable return within 30 days, deletion plus written certification) and is a targeted addition appended after 4(c)(iv) rather than a rewrite of existing text. The precedence sentence over 4(c)(iv) is a necessary and minimal addition, since the existing destroy-at-election right would otherwise defeat the data-return obligation identified in the rationale. Comment is accurate, concise, in the required first-person plural tone with the [Playbook] prefix, explains the change, and offers the 90-day fallback; deterministic checks corroborate that transition/data-return language is present in the redline.

quote: (ix) it is now and throughout the Term shall comply with all applicable Laws in connection with the operation of its business and the performance of its obligations hereunder or the provision of the Service
rationale:
Compliant at or above the preferred position; no redline proposed.

Scope: Section 9(b) contains genuine express Vendor warranties — the Service "will perform in all material respects to industry standards" (9(b)(ii)), services will "be free from errors that materially affect their utility" (9(b)(vi)), no viruses/Trojan Horses/worms or other harmful routines (9(b)(iv)), and compliance with all applicable Laws (9(b)(ix)), plus IP non-infringement and ownership warranties. That matches the preferred position's substantive scope (professional performance, conformance, compliance with laws, no malicious code).

Period (addressing the failed numeric check): the warranties are drafted as continuing "represents, warrants and covenants" obligations running "now and throughout the Term" rather than expiring after a fixed window. The Term is expressed in years, not days: paragraph 4(a) sets an Initial Term of "one (1) year from the Effective Date," automatically renewing for additional 1-year terms. The effective warranty duration is therefore at least twelve (12) months and, on renewal, longer — meeting the preferred 12-month software period and exceeding the 90-day services period and the fallback entirely. The deterministic period check failed only because no standalone "90 days"/"12 months" warranty window is recited; the absence of that cut-off is what makes the clause better for us, so it is a false negative and not a ground to redline.

Disclaimer: Section 13 does not swallow the express warranty. It is bracketed by "Except as expressly set forth herein" and "except for the representations and warranties set forth in this Agreement," confining the "as is"/"as available" language to implied warranties (merchantability, fitness, course of dealing). Walk-away "AS IS" territory is ruled out.

Noted, not flagged: there is no express repair/replace/refund remedy sentence. Consistent with the playbook's treatment of minor sub-elements, we note rather than flag it — general contract remedies remain available, the Section 7 cap excludes only consequential damages, paragraph 4(b) gives a 30-day cure/termination right for material breach, and Section 11(a)(iv) indemnifies us for Kubient's breach of any warranty. Importing the model remedy sentence would risk converting that open relief into a narrower Vendor-elected exclusive remedy, so pressing it would work against our interests.

verification.notes: Claimed status is compliant and the rendered redline is byte-identical to the original paragraphs with no comment, which is the expected output for a compliant finding. The cited text supports compliance: Section 9(b) contains genuine express Vendor warranties covering performance to industry standards (9(b)(ii)), freedom from errors materially affecting utility (9(b)(vi)), no viruses/malicious routines (9(b)(iv)) and compliance with applicable Laws (9(b)(ix)) — matching the preferred position's substantive scope. Duration analysis is sound: the warranties are continuing 'now and throughout the Term' obligations, and the Term is a 1-year Initial Term with automatic 1-year renewals, so the effective coverage equals or exceeds the preferred 12-month/90-day windows; the deterministic period check is satisfied. The Section 13 disclaimer is bracketed by 'Except as expressly set forth herein' and 'except for the representations and warranties set forth in this Agreement,' so it does not swallow the express warranties and walk-away 'AS IS' territory is ruled out. The absent repair/replace/refund sentence is properly noted rather than flagged: it is a sub-element short of preferred wording, and importing a Vendor-elected exclusive remedy would narrow the customer's existing general remedies, cure/termination right and warranty-breach indemnity — consistent with the instruction not to flag clauses that benefit our party.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have added an express limb confirming that Kubient's indemnity covers third-party claims that the Services, Auction Platform or deliverables infringe intellectual property rights. This coverage is already implicit through the warranty-breach limb and Kubient's non-infringement warranty, so we regard this as a clarification rather than a change in the bargain, and it avoids our having to prove a warranty breach before the defence obligation is triggered.

ops.text: any allegation or claim that the Services, the Auction Platform or any deliverables provided hereunder by Kubient infringe, misappropriate or violate any patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret or other intellectual property right of any third party.

proposal.summary: Add an express third-party IP infringement limb to Kubient's indemnity in Section 10.

quote: (iv) Kubient's breach of any representation or warranty under this Agreement or (v) the acts or omissions of Kubient or a third party hired by, employed, retained or under Kubient control with respect to Kubient's obligations hereunder.
rationale:
Section 10 contains a genuine Vendor indemnity, but it has no express third-party IP-infringement limb. Kubient's limbs are: (i) the Services, (ii) the Auction Platform, (iii) the Creative (knowledge-qualified), (iv) breach of any representation or warranty, and (v) the acts or omissions of Kubient or its subcontractors. IP infringement is reached only derivatively - through limb (iv) read together with the non-infringement warranty at p0033 ("the Service and any deliverables provided hereunder by Kubient do not and shall not infringe, misappropriate or violate any patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, publicity, privacy or other rights of any third party"), and through the broad "arising out of or in connection with the Services" language. That derivative route is materially weaker than the preferred position's express IP limb: on limb (iv) the defence obligation is keyed to a breach of warranty, so Kubient can argue AP must first establish breach before defence is owed, whereas an express infringement limb triggers on the mere allegation. Given this is the critical IP indemnity, we take the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position: inserting limb (vi) covering any allegation or claim that the Services, Auction Platform or deliverables infringe, misappropriate or violate third-party IP rights. The redline is clarifying rather than expansionary, since the same exposure already sits with Kubient via p0033 and limb (iv), which is how we would defend the change in negotiation.

The rest of the rule is satisfied and is not redlined. Kubient "agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer and its officers, directors, managers, members, agents, and employees" from all third-party Claims including reasonable attorneys' fees (p0047). Breach of law is covered via limb (iv) plus the compliance-with-Law warranty (p0041); Vendor-caused data incidents, gross negligence and wilful misconduct are covered by limb (v). Standard procedure is present at p0053-p0055 (prompt notice with no forfeiture for delay, indemnitor control of defence and settlement subject to consent for liability-admitting settlements, cooperation at the indemnitor's cost). p0027 carves indemnification out of the consequential-damages exclusion and no cap is applied, so the fallback's 3x annual fees super-cap is unnecessary and we do not seek it. Direction is correct on our side: AP's indemnity (p0052) is keyed to its own Content and Properties, its own unauthorised use, breach and acts or omissions, and does not indemnify Kubient for Kubient's Services, so no walk-away scenario arises and no narrowing of AP's indemnity is required.

Two minor sub-elements remain noted rather than flagged: the "to the best of its knowledge" qualifier on the Creative limb (p0050), and AP's indemnity extending slightly beyond Customer-provided content and breach of law to unauthorised use and breach of any representation or warranty.

verification.notes: Over-flagging: the existing Section 10(a) is a genuine Vendor-side indemnity covering 'all third-party allegations, claims, actions ... arising out of or in connection with (i) the Services; (ii) the Auction Platform', which on its face captures a third-party allegation that the Services or Platform infringe IP. Combined with the express non-infringement warranty at p0033 and the warranty-breach limb (iv), the clause does not 'exclude IP infringement' — the trigger under the guidance for a deviation. On the playbook's classification semantics the clause meets (indeed exceeds) the fallback (Vendor IP indemnity, no cap needed because indemnification is carved out of the damages exclusion and uncapped) and materially the preferred position: the finding's own rationale confirms defence obligation, breach-of-law, data-incident, gross negligence/wilful misconduct coverage, standard procedure (p0053-p0055), and a suitably narrow Customer indemnity. The absence of an express standalone IP limb is a wording/mechanic refinement to be noted in the rationale, not redlined. The redline is not actionable as rendered: the new text is appended after the full stop ending limb (v) with no '(vi)' label and no connecting 'or', leaving a dangling sentence fragment inside the enumerated list rather than the clean limb (vi) described in the rationale. Correct disposition would be a 'compliant' finding noting that IP infringement is reached through the broad 'arising out of or in connection with the Services' limb plus the p0033 warranty, with the knowledge qualifier on the Creative limb flagged as a minor sub-element.
